bibl.title: The deep sea is a major sink for microplastic debris

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: where the manufactured plastic that surveys cannot account for has gone, and whether deep-sea sediment holds it
span.quote: However, despite the durability of plastic, and the exponential increase in its production, monitoring data show limited evidence of concomitant increasing concentrations in marine habitats. There appears to be a considerable proportion of the manufactured plastic that is unaccounted for in surveys tracking the fate of environmental plastics. Even the discovery of widespread accumulation of microscopic fragments (microplastics) in oceanic gyres and shallow water sediments is unable to explain the missing fraction.

span.label: how abundant and how widespread microplastic contamination is across a range of deep-sea depths and locations
span.quote: Here, we present results from a global analysis of deep-sea sediment collected by two independent research teams during seven research cruises between September 2001 and August 2012, in the Mediterranean Sea, SW Indian Ocean and NE Atlantic Ocean (spanning subtropical to subpolar waters). The purpose of this study was to quantify the abundance and extent of microplastic contamination at a range of depths and locations in the deep sea.

span.label: microplastic fibres in all 12 sediment cores and all four coral samples from three oceans, at up to four orders of magnitude greater abundance per unit volume than heavily contaminated surface water - and the demonstration that the one previous deep-sea survey found little because it did not count fibres
span.quote: Here, we show that deep-sea sediments are a likely sink for microplastics. Microplastic, in the form of fibres, was up to four orders of magnitude more abundant (per unit volume) in deep-sea sediments from the Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea and Indian Ocean than in contaminated sea-surface waters. Our results show evidence for a large and hitherto unknown repository of microplastics. The dominance of microfibres points to a previously underreported and unsampled plastic fraction.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Identification by FT-IR spectroscopy confirmed that microplastics were abundant in all 12 sediment samples and all coral samples. The microplastics were all fibrous in shape, were commonly 2–3 mm in length and less than 0.1 mm in diameter (electronic supplementary material, figure S1). Plastic microfibre abundance in the sediments ranged from 1.4 to 40 pieces per 50 ml (mean±s.e.: 13.4±3.5; figure 2), and samples from four locations in the Indian Ocean showed that microplastics had also accumulated on the surface of octocorals.

span.label: accumulation of plastic microfibres on the deep-sea floor - a repository large enough to bear on the missing-plastic budget, and unsampled until now
span.quote: The prevalence of plastic microfibres in all sediment cores and on all coral colonies examined suggests this contaminant is ubiquitous in the deep sea. Furthermore, the wide variety of polymer types detected reveals that the accumulation and deposition of microfibres in the deep sea is complex and that they arise from a variety of domestic and industrial sources.

span.label: sediment cores and coral specimens from seven cruises by two independent teams, density-separated with NaCl or Ludox-TM 40, picked under a binocular microscope and identified by FT-IR against a spectral library that had the investigators' own clothing and gloves added to it
span.term: sediment cores and coral specimens from seven cruises by two independent teams, density-separated with NaCl or Ludox-TM 40, picked under a binocular microscope and identified by FT-IR against a spectral library that had the investigators' own clothing and gloves added to it
span.quote: We added the spectra of potential contaminants, such as those from waterproofs and laboratory gloves used during sample collection and processing, to the Plymouth University FT-IR library in order to eventually eliminate any contamination from the data. No matches with these materials were found in any of the samples.

span.label: a positively buoyant plastic floats when it enters the sea, and fouling by organisms and adherence of particles change its density over weeks to months until it sinks - so the compartment a plastic is found in is a function of how long it has been there
span.term: buoyancy reversed by what grows on the particle
span.quote: Plastics can be denser (e.g. acrylic) or lighter (e.g. polypropylene) than seawater. Those that are buoyant float when first entering the sea, so historically attention has focused on the accumulation on shorelines and at the sea surface. However, because of fouling by organisms and adherence of particles, positively buoyant plastics can, over a timescale of weeks to months, become negatively buoyant and sink.

span.label: surface tension and currents hold most plastic at the surface; colonisation, adherence to phytoplankton and aggregation into marine snow bind fibres into larger, faster-settling particles, which is how a fibre reaches 3500 m
span.quote: Some negatively buoyant particles will sink; however, because of surface tension and oceanographic currents, most plastics are initially held at the sea surface. Colonization by organisms, adherence to phytoplankton and the aggregation with organic debris and small particles in the form of marine snow will eventually enhance settling.

span.label: dense shelf water cascading, coastal storms, offshore convection and saline subduction all move large volumes of particle-loaded water downslope, carrying a full spectrum of grain sizes together with litter and contaminants, and submarine canyons concentrate the flow
span.term: canyons as conduits for particle-loaded water
span.quote: In addition, a number of oceanographic processes could aid in the transfer of microplastics to depth. These processes include dense shelf water cascading, severe coastal storms, offshore convection and saline subduction. All these induce vertical and horizontal transfers of large volumes of particle loaded waters, including a full spectrum of grain sizes (from sand to clay), as well as litter and contaminants, from shallow ocean layers and coastal regions to deeper ones, with submarine canyons acting as preferential conduits.

span.label: the fibres are the most numerous particle type in shallow habitats, so a protocol that does not enumerate fibres returns a low number from sediment that contains many - the difference between the two deep-sea reports is a decision about what to write down, and the authors demonstrated it on split samples rather than arguing it
span.term: a recording rule deciding an abundance
span.quote: We ran a preliminary trial to compare methods used by both studies, by splitting some of our deep-sea sediment samples and analysing them using both approaches. We found that our approach and our recording of microfibres yielded substantially greater abundance of microplastic particles, whereas the other method underestimated the microplastic concentration (electronic supplementary material).

span.label: no statistical comparison of abundance or composition between samples is possible - the authors name the lack of replicates, the small sample size and the methodological differences, and decline to make one
span.quote: Because of the lack of replicate samples, small sample size and differences in methodology, no attempt can be made to statistically compare microplastic abundance and composition between samples and make conclusions on patterns observed. However, we can and do compare the mean abundance reported here with that of other studies, highlighting the ubiquity of the microplastic presence and emphasizing that the microplastics reported were all fibres.

span.label: the four-orders-of-magnitude comparison with surface water is qualitative, because surface waters and sediments are sampled by different methods
span.quote: While different methods are used to sample surface waters and sediments, a qualitative comparison indicated four orders of magnitude greater abundance per unit volume in deep-sea sediments compared with heavily contaminated surface water gyres

span.label: whether fibres dominate sediment and fragments dominate the surface is a real distribution or an artefact of sampling method cannot be determined at present
span.quote: It is notable that fibres represented the largest proportion of microplastics seen in other studies based on sediment analyses, whereas sea-surface studies most often report larger fragments. At present, it is not possible to determine whether this is a true reflection of the relative abundance of different microplastic fractions in different substrata or if it is an artefact of differences in sampling methodology.

span.label: the precise origin of individual microplastic debris cannot currently be established, although the polymer types point to diverse domestic and industrial sources
span.quote: The plastic polymers found in this study are used in a wide range of domestic and industrial applications, including packaging, textiles and electronics, which indicates diverse sources. However, the precise origin of individual microplastic debris cannot currently be established.

span.label: the coral samples were never quantitative - fibres were not extracted exhaustively and only presence or absence was recorded
span.quote: The corals were of different sizes, and not all fibres present on the corals were removed, therefore just the presence or absence of microplastic accumulation on living coral was recorded.

span.label: rayon, which the authors state is not a plastic, is included in the counts and supplies 56.9% of the fibres reported
span.quote: Rayon is not a plastic, but we include it in our results, because it is a man-made semi-synthetic material and widely reported as present in the marine environment. It is used in cigarette filters, personal hygiene products and clothing, and is introduced to the marine environment through sewage, including from the washing of clothes.

span.label: the 4 billion fibres per square kilometre figure is an extrapolation, offered on the most conservative estimates
span.quote: Our data show that, if extrapolated and using the most conservative estimates, 4 billion fibres per km2 would be present in Indian Ocean seamount sediment.

span.label: few studies examine the biological effects of microplastics at all, so what this abundance implies for harm is not established here
span.quote: In contrast with studies on the effects of large plastic debris, which mostly document entanglement and ingestion, there are few studies examining the biological effects of microplastics. A range of organisms are known to ingest microplastics, and there is concern this could result in physical and/or toxicological harm. The extent to which microplastics could have harmful effects will most likely be influenced by their relative abundance.

span.label: particle-transport mechanisms carried from physical oceanography - cascading, convection, saline subduction, canyon funnelling and Taylor columns - to explain how a textile fibre reaches the abyssal floor
span.quote: In addition, a number of oceanographic processes could aid in the transfer of microplastics to depth. These processes include dense shelf water cascading, severe coastal storms, offshore convection and saline subduction. All these induce vertical and horizontal transfers of large volumes of particle loaded waters, including a full spectrum of grain sizes (from sand to clay), as well as litter and contaminants, from shallow ocean layers and coastal regions to deeper ones, with submarine canyons acting as preferential conduits.

span.label: marine snow, a biological-oceanography construct for aggregated organic debris, used as the vehicle that makes a buoyant synthetic fibre settle
span.quote: Some negatively buoyant particles will sink; however, because of surface tension and oceanographic currents, most plastics are initially held at the sea surface. Colonization by organisms, adherence to phytoplankton and the aggregation with organic debris and small particles in the form of marine snow will eventually enhance settling.

span.label: every preservation and processing fluid filtered through a 32 um sieve before use, and the fresh and salt water supplies sampled for an hour daily and screened for fibres
span.note: eliminates: the laboratory's own water as the source of the fibres - a fibre that arrived in the rinse would be indistinguishable from one that arrived from the seafloor · outcome: held
span.quote: All preservation and processing fluids were filtered through a 32 μm sieve prior to adding them to the sediment. Filtered (5 μm) fresh water and seawater were used to wash equipment, and water from both fresh and salt water supplies was sampled for 1 h daily through a 32 μm sieve and screened for the presence of microplastic fibres, but none was seen.

span.label: the spectra of the actual waterproofs and laboratory gloves used during collection and processing added to the FT-IR reference library, so that a fibre shed from them would be identified as such rather than as an unknown polymer
span.note: eliminates: the investigators' own equipment as the source of the identified polymers - without the spectra in the library a glove fibre matches nothing and is simply an unmatched particle · outcome: held
span.quote: We added the spectra of potential contaminants, such as those from waterproofs and laboratory gloves used during sample collection and processing, to the Plymouth University FT-IR library in order to eventually eliminate any contamination from the data. No matches with these materials were found in any of the samples.

span.label: all residue sediment checked for the larger plastic particles the previous deep-sea study described, not only for the fibres this study was looking for
span.note: eliminates: this protocol having simply traded one blind spot for another - the check asks whether the particles the other method counts were present and missed · outcome: held
span.quote: In addition, we checked all residue sediment for the larger plastic particles described in Van Cauwenberghe et al.. None were seen. Protocols were implemented to prevent plastic contamination from the processing environment and controls to monitor air and water supplies were taken during all processing phases.

span.label: two extraction methods used by two independent teams, with the specific gravities of the separating substances reported against each other - 1.2 for NaCl, 1.16 for Ludox
span.note: eliminates: either laboratory's separation chemistry as the source of the result, to the extent that a float separation is characterised by its density · outcome: partial
span.quote: The substances chosen to isolate the fibres (NaCl or Ludox-TM 40) had similar specific gravities, namely 1.2 and 1.16, for PU and NHM, respectively. We are therefore confident that the same fractions and types of microplastics were isolated.

span.label: their own deep-sea samples split and run through both this protocol and the protocol of the one previous deep-sea study, rather than comparing published numbers
span.note: eliminates: a real difference between sites as the explanation of the disagreement with the previous report - the same sediment cannot differ from itself · outcome: held
span.quote: We ran a preliminary trial to compare methods used by both studies, by splitting some of our deep-sea sediment samples and analysing them using both approaches. We found that our approach and our recording of microfibres yielded substantially greater abundance of microplastic particles, whereas the other method underestimated the microplastic concentration (electronic supplementary material).

span.label: damp filter paper exposed to the laboratory air whenever samples were open, as a check on airborne contamination during processing
span.note: eliminates: airborne microplastic fibres settling into the samples during processing - the whole finding is fibres in deep-sea sediment, and the laboratory air is the rival source · outcome: held
span.quote: All sample processing (extraction and picking) was conducted in a clean laboratory, where extreme care was taken to avoid any contamination. Checks for contamination during processing were made by exposing damp filter paper to the air in the laboratory, whenever samples were open to the laboratory environment.

span.label: natural fibre clothing only, with 100% cotton coats and headwear and latex gloves, for all laboratory processing and for the JC76T cruise
span.note: eliminates: synthetic fibres shed from the handlers' own clothing, which would be indistinguishable from the microplastic being counted · outcome: held
span.quote: As an additional precaution, those handling the samples wore only natural fibre clothing, and were protected with 100% cotton laboratory coats and headwear, and latex gloves, for all laboratory processing and during the JC76T research cruise.

span.label: FT-IR acceptance thresholds on the spectral quality index - 0.7 and above accepted, 0.6 to 0.7 inspected individually, below 0.6 rejected
span.note: eliminates: false polymer identifications from poor-quality FT-IR spectra, with the middle band inspected by hand rather than accepted or dropped wholesale · outcome: held
span.quote: Matches with quality index greater than or equal to 0.7 were accepted. Matches with quality index less than 0.7, but greater than or equal to 0.6 were individually inspected and interpreted based on the closeness of their absorption frequencies to those of chemical bonds in the known polymers. Matches with quality index less than 0.6 were rejected.

span.label: microplastics
span.quote: Here, we show that deep-sea sediments are a likely sink for microplastics. Microplastic, in the form of fibres, was up to four orders of magnitude more abundant (per unit volume) in deep-sea sediments from the Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea and Indian Ocean than in contaminated sea-surface waters. Our results show evidence for a large and hitherto unknown repository of microplastics. The dominance of microfibres points to a previously underreported and unsampled plastic fraction.

span.label: Rayon
span.quote: Rayon, which is a man-made non-plastic polymer, was detected in all the samples (electronic supplementary material, figure S2a). It contributed to 56.9% of the total number of fibres seen and was more than twice as abundant as polyester (electronic supplementary material, figure S2b).

span.label: deep-sea microplastic abundance - UNDER THE PREVIOUS PROTOCOL: very low, from a method that did not enumerate fibres at all
span.quote: There has only been one previous report of microplastics in the deep sea, which documented very low abundance. The previous study employed different separation methods to those used here and critically did not enumerate microplastic fibres, which are the most numerous type of particle present in shallow water habitats and in some biota.

span.label: deep-sea microplastic abundance - UNDER THIS PROTOCOL, ON THE SAME SPLIT SAMPLES: substantially greater, with the other method shown to underestimate
span.quote: We ran a preliminary trial to compare methods used by both studies, by splitting some of our deep-sea sediment samples and analysing them using both approaches. We found that our approach and our recording of microfibres yielded substantially greater abundance of microplastic particles, whereas the other method underestimated the microplastic concentration (electronic supplementary material).

span.label: the reported count - AS A COUNT OF FIBRES: 13.4 pieces per 50 ml, 1.4 to 40 across the cores, every one of them fibrous in shape
span.quote: Identification by FT-IR spectroscopy confirmed that microplastics were abundant in all 12 sediment samples and all coral samples. span.label: the reported count - AS A COUNT OF PLASTIC: a minority of it, since rayon is 56.9% of the fibres and the authors state that rayon is not a plastic
span.quote: Rayon is not a plastic, but we include it in our results, because it is a man-made semi-synthetic material and widely reported as present in the marine environment. span.quote: Here, we show that deep-sea sediments are a likely sink for microplastics. Microplastic, in the form of fibres, was up to four orders of magnitude more abundant (per unit volume) in deep-sea sediments from the Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea and Indian Ocean than in contaminated sea-surface waters. Our results show evidence for a large and hitherto unknown repository of microplastics. The dominance of microfibres points to a previously underreported and unsampled plastic fraction.

span.label: the comparison with surface water - AS THE DISCUSSION QUALIFIES IT: qualitative, because different methods sample the two compartments
span.quote: While different methods are used to sample surface waters and sediments, a qualitative comparison indicated four orders of magnitude greater abundance per unit volume in deep-sea sediments compared with heavily contaminated surface water gyres

span.label: critiques → routine environmental monitoring of plastic debris, which has produced little evidence of the expected increase and leaves temporal trends unresolved in most datasets because microplastics were not included
span.quote: However, despite extensive environmental monitoring, there is little evidence of the expected increasing abundance of plastic debris in natural habitats. Only two studies report an increase over time. Both these papers focused on microplastics, which have not typically been included in routine monitoring, and are likely to represent a largely undocumented accumulation of plastic debris. Yet, even for microplastic pollution, temporal trends are unresolved in the majority of datasets.

span.label: qualifies → the one previous report of microplastics in the deep sea, whose very low abundance is attributed here to a protocol that did not enumerate fibres - tested on split samples, not asserted
span.quote: We ran a preliminary trial to compare methods used by both studies, by splitting some of our deep-sea sediment samples and analysing them using both approaches. We found that our approach and our recording of microfibres yielded substantially greater abundance of microplastic particles, whereas the other method underestimated the microplastic concentration (electronic supplementary material).

span.label: extends → Van Cauwenberghe et al., with which this paper is offered jointly as the first evidence of global sinks for microplastic debris - the same study it corrects on method
span.quote: In addition, we checked all residue sediment for the larger plastic particles described in Van Cauwenberghe et al.. None were seen. span.label: critiques → the field's methodological inconsistency, which the authors say must be fixed before robust temporal and spatial comparisons are possible at all
span.quote: It is now crucial to establish consistent methodologies to allow robust temporal and spatial comparisons, to address how abundance and composition vary with depth, location, topography and habitat, and apply these data to the already complex oceanographic transport models available for some oceans, which have successfully been used to predict surface plastic accumulation.

span.quote: Of the remaining fibres, polyester was the most prevalent (53.4%), followed by other plastics (34.1%), which included polyamides and acetate, then acrylic (12.4%) (figure 2).

span.label: the range of plastic microfibre abundance across the sediment cores, in pieces per 50 ml
span.quote: Identification by FT-IR spectroscopy confirmed that microplastics were abundant in all 12 sediment samples and all coral samples. The microplastics were all fibrous in shape, were commonly 2–3 mm in length and less than 0.1 mm in diameter (electronic supplementary material, figure S1). Plastic microfibre abundance in the sediments ranged from 1.4 to 40 pieces per 50 ml (mean±s.e.: 13.4±3.5; figure 2), and samples from four locations in the Indian Ocean showed that microplastics had also accumulated on the surface of octocorals.

span.label: fibres per square kilometre of Indian Ocean seamount sediment, extrapolated on the most conservative estimates
span.quote: Our data show that, if extrapolated and using the most conservative estimates, 4 billion fibres per km2 would be present in Indian Ocean seamount sediment.

span.label: the specific gravity of the Ludox-TM 40 separation, against 1.2 for the NaCl one - the number the two teams' comparability rests on
span.quote: The substances chosen to isolate the fibres (NaCl or Ludox-TM 40) had similar specific gravities, namely 1.2 and 1.16, for PU and NHM, respectively. We are therefore confident that the same fractions and types of microplastics were isolated.

span.label: mean
span.quote: Identification by FT-IR spectroscopy confirmed that microplastics were abundant in all 12 sediment samples and all coral samples. The microplastics were all fibrous in shape, were commonly 2–3 mm in length and less than 0.1 mm in diameter (electronic supplementary material, figure S1). Plastic microfibre abundance in the sediments ranged from 1.4 to 40 pieces per 50 ml (mean±s.e.: 13.4±3.5; figure 2), and samples from four locations in the Indian Ocean showed that microplastics had also accumulated on the surface of octocorals.

span.label: microplastic abundance
span.quote: Because of the lack of replicate samples, small sample size and differences in methodology, no attempt can be made to statistically compare microplastic abundance and composition between samples and make conclusions on patterns observed. However, we can and do compare the mean abundance reported here with that of other studies, highlighting the ubiquity of the microplastic presence and emphasizing that the microplastics reported were all fibres.

span.label: quality index
span.quote: Matches with quality index greater than or equal to 0.7 were accepted. Matches with quality index less than 0.7, but greater than or equal to 0.6 were individually inspected and interpreted based on the closeness of their absorption frequencies to those of chemical bonds in the known polymers. Matches with quality index less than 0.6 were rejected.
